content: Brittle nails, also known as onychorrhexis, refer to a condition where the nails are fragile and prone to frequent breaking or splitting along their length. Causes: Brittle nails can result from various underlying factors, including infections or nutritional disorders. They may also serve as a clinical indicator of several medical conditions, such as iron deficiency, anemia, hypothyroidism, impaired kidney function, circulation problems, or biotin deficiency. Specific Causes (in alphabetical order): Anemia: A condition characterized by a deficiency of red blood cells or hemoglobin, which can weaken nail structure. Anorexia nervosa: A severe eating disorder that can lead to malnutrition and brittle nails. Biotin deficiency: A lack of this essential B-vitamin can impair keratin production, affecting nail strength. Bulimia: Another eating disorder that can result in nutritional deficiencies impacting nail health. Circulation problems: Poor blood flow can deprive nails of essential nutrients and oxygen. Excessive exposure to strong soaps and water: Prolonged contact with harsh chemicals can strip nails of their natural oils, leading to brittleness. Hypothyroidism: An underactive thyroid gland can slow metabolic processes, including nail growth and repair. Impaired kidney function: Chronic kidney disease can lead to metabolic imbalances that affect nail integrity. Infections: Fungal or bacterial infections can weaken the nail structure. Iron deficiency: A lack of sufficient iron can compromise the production of healthy nails. Nail polish remover: Frequent use of acetone-based removers can dry out and damage nails. Nutritional disorders: General malnutrition or deficiencies in essential nutrients can weaken nails. Oral retinoid therapy: Medications like isotretinoin can cause nail fragility as a side effect. Witkop syndrome: A rare genetic condition associated with nail abnormalities. Diagnosis: During a physical examination, brittle nails may present as nails that exhibit visible splitting or longitudinal cracks. This characteristic splitting is a hallmark feature of the condition. Epidemiology and Demographics: Brittle nails are a relatively common condition, affecting up to 20% of the general population. Treatment: Primary Prevention: Several strategies have been proposed to prevent brittle nails. These include: Taking vitamin supplements to address potential deficiencies. Consuming gelatin or glucosamine, which may support nail health. Reducing the use of nail polish to minimize chemical exposure. Ensuring proper hydration and moisture to maintain nail flexibility and strength.
